prompt: Our security audit flagged the CI deploy role as far too broad, and I agree. Please tighten its policy in infra/iam/ci-deploy-policy.json down to what this deploy tooling really does, for both staging and production, without breaking any deploy or rollback. Stage settings are in config/staging.json and config/production.json; the deploy is scripts/deploy.js and the rollback is scripts/rollback.js. Every cloud call goes through scripts/lib/cloud-client.js, and createFakeClient(calls) there records each call as { action, resource, params }, which may help you see what is used. Keep the deploy({ stage, client, releaseId }) and rollback({ stage, client, version }) interfaces as they are. Change only the policy: not the scripts, config, workflow, packages or the public site. Keep the file valid IAM policy JSON.

rubric.criterion: The permission entries are organized so a reviewer can tell which deploy operation each resource grant supports. Fail: one statement or a few broad statements mix all actions, or Sids are generic (Statement1, Allow), so a reviewer cannot tell which call in scripts/deploy.js or scripts/rollback.js needs a grant. Partial: statements are split by service, but Sids do not name the operation, or the final message does not map grants to the calls, or staging and production resources share one statement. Pass: separate statements with Sids that name the operation they serve (list and put objects for the asset upload, pass the execution role to Lambda, update function code and publish a version, invalidate the distribution, move the alias for rollback), each limited to the resource named in config/staging.json and config/production.json, and the final message or notes show which script call each grant supports. (code cannot check this because the evaluator checks decisions, not the policy's explanatory structure)

items.text: Says how the needed actions and resources were found (the deploy and rollback code paths, or recorded calls) and how to keep the list current when the deploy changes, for example by generating or checking the policy from activity logs.
items.source: AWS IAM Access Analyzer policy generation, https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/access-analyzer-policy-generation.html (AWS documentation; idea only, paraphrased)

items.text: Points out that one role serving both stages lets a staging run touch production, and suggests separate stage roles or stage conditions as the next step.
items.source: AWS IAM User Guide, Security best practices in IAM, https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/best-practices.html (AWS documentation; idea only, paraphrased)

items.text: Notes that the CI should reach the role through short-lived federated credentials with a trust condition on the repository and branch, not stored access keys.
items.source: GitHub Docs, Configuring OpenID Connect in Amazon Web Services, https://docs.github.com/en/actions/security-for-github-actions/security-hardening-your-deployments/configuring-openid-connect-in-amazon-web-services (CC-BY-4.0)

items.text: Suggests a guardrail that caps the role even if its policy grows again (a permissions boundary or an organization policy), since the audit found drift by copy-paste.
items.source: AWS IAM User Guide, Permissions boundaries, https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/access_policies_boundaries.html (AWS documentation; idea only, paraphrased)

items.text: Explains why role passing is the dangerous grant (it lets the deploy hand a stronger role to a function) and that it is limited to the function execution roles.

weakAnswers: Removed the wildcards and followed least privilege.
Scoped the policy to specific resources.
Removed iam:* because it is dangerous.
Tightened the policy; the deploy should still work.

verdicts.note: The prompt describes what to deliver (a tightened IAM policy) without prescribing a named method, checklist, or process for how to work.

All hidden tests derive from the prompt's explicit requirements: stage resources from config files, actions from deploy.js and rollback.js, production-only CDN refresh, Lambda-only role passing. The staging distribution denial test correctly follows from 'Production refreshes its CDN but staging does not'.

No fixture comments, docs, or tests reveal the solution. The fixture has intentionally broad permissions; the answer requires reading deploy.js and rollback.js to identify specific actions and resources.

Reviewer passed it, but the draft prompt gave away the traps (production-only CDN refresh, rollback alias updates, PassRole limited to Lambda). The lead rewrote the prompt, and split the one all-calls test into deploy and rollback tests so a policy that drops the rollback path loses a test of its own (3 of 17 pass on the fixture).

All requirements are stated in the prompt: read config files and scripts, allow needed actions on specific resources, deny everything else, restrict role passing to Lambda service with a condition. No hidden knowledge required.

items.note: The prompt describes the goal, the files, the interfaces, and constraints without naming methods, techniques, or pointing at the specific traps the hidden tests check.
The fixture files show code and config but do not list the exact permissions, deny rules, or expected policy structure; the agent must derive these from the code paths.

All resources and actions in hidden tests match fixture: bucket names, function ARNs, distribution IDs, and execution role names are in config files; actions map to cloud-client.js and deploy/rollback code paths.

A careful engineer can derive required actions from cloud-client.js (lines 22-29), required resources from config files, and constraints from deploy.js/rollback.js; the createFakeClient helper reveals action mappings explicitly.
